title: Nine Fours. Zero Sixes. The Most Important Innings of Vaibhav Sooryavanshi's Life.
excerpt: The 15-year-old IPL sensation hit 44 off 22 balls against Afghanistan A without clearing the boundary once — and silenced every critic who called him a slogger.
body:
The numbers on their own are absurd. Forty-four runs off 22 balls, a strike rate of 200, nine boundaries through the gaps. But the number that matters most is the one that reads zero. Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, the boy who hit 72 sixes in IPL 2026 — more than Chris Gayle managed in any single season — did not clear the rope once.

This was not a limited innings. It was a deliberate one.

In the second match of the India A tri-series against Afghanistan A at the Rangiri Dambulla International Stadium on Thursday, the 15-year-old left-hander played an innings that will matter far more to his international career than any of his IPL pyrotechnics. He punched through extra cover. He bisected the gap between point and backward point. He drove along the carpet with the wrists of a batsman twice his age. And he did it on a sluggish Dambulla wicket that offered nothing for free.

## The Redemption

Two days earlier, Sooryavanshi had looked every inch the teenage debutant. Against Sri Lanka A in the first match of the tri-series, he was dismissed for 14 off 12 balls, undone by Chamika Karunaratne's clever cutters and slower bouncers. He attempted to loft Mohammad Shiraz over mid-off and found a diving Sahan Arachchige instead. India A were 16 for 2 inside five overs, and the boy wonder walked back to the pavilion looking like a boy.

Thursday was the answer. Opening alongside Prabhsimran Singh, Sooryavanshi combined with his partner for 74 runs in just seven overs, setting the tone for an innings that would see India A post a commanding total. Singh went on to make 84 off 69, but it was the teenager's 22-ball blitz that broke the game open.

## The Manjrekar Verdict

Former India batter Sanjay Manjrekar, not a man given to easy praise, was watching from home and could not contain himself.

"India A is in SL, pitch not as flat as in the IPL & it's not T20 cricket," Manjrekar wrote on X. "So watching Vaibhav Suryavanshi in different batting conditions. And I am excited! He is not just your T20 slogger. He can be a one day phenomenon too! Special talent!"

That last phrase — "not just your T20 slogger" — is precisely the label Sooryavanshi needed to shed. In IPL 2026, his 776 runs at a strike rate of 237 made him the youngest Orange Cap winner in tournament history. But the knock-on question was obvious: could a 15-year-old who thrived on flat Indian decks and short boundaries survive on surfaces that demanded patience?

## The Road to Dublin

The answer matters because Sooryavanshi is not just an India A tourist. He has already been named in India's senior T20I squad for the tours of Ireland and England, starting June 28. If he plays in Belfast or at The Oval, he will become one of the youngest Indians to earn a senior cap in any format.

Shreyas Iyer, who has been named T20I captain for the Ireland series, will have the teenager in his dressing room. So will the other young guns — Tilak Varma, who captained India A in Dambulla with growing assurance, and Ruturaj Gaikwad, who smashed a hundred in the first match after being drafted as a late replacement for the injured Riyan Parag.

For the NRI community in Ireland and the UK, this could be an unmissable window. Dublin's Civil Service Cricket Club will host the T20Is on June 26 and 28, and London's Oval will follow for the England series. Tickets for Indo-Irish cricket matches in Belfast and Dublin tend to sell fast, driven heavily by the Indian diaspora in the tech corridors of Dublin and London.

## Why It Matters

Indian cricket has produced prodigies before — Tendulkar, Kohli, Gill — but none of them had to navigate the gap between T20 stardom and international readiness at 15. Sooryavanshi is doing it in real time, with the entire cricket world watching.

Thursday's innings in Dambulla was not his most spectacular. It was not his highest score. It was not even a fifty. But it may have been the most important knock of his young life, because it proved that behind the sixes and the swagger, there is a cricketer who can bat.

The next stop is Ireland. The kid is ready.
